etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English diverten, Old French divertir (“to turn or go different ways, part, separate, divert”), from Latin di- (“apart”) + vertere (“to turn”); see verse.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To turn aside from a course.

quote.citation: 1960 February, R. C. Riley, “The London-Birmingham services - Past, Present and Future”, in Trains Illustrated, page 99:
quote.text: Many of the remaining trains have been retimed and where possible freight trains have also been diverted to alternative routes.

quote.citation: [1644], [John Milton], Of Education. To Master Samuel Hartlib, [London:  […]  Thomas Underhill and/or Thomas Johnson], →OCLC:
quote.text: that crude apple that diverted Eve

definitions.definition: (transitive) To entertain or amuse (by diverting the attention)

quote.text: We are amused by a tale, diverted by a comedy.

quote.citation: 1973 December 29, Jonathan Cross, “The Fag In The Fifth Row”, in Gay Community News, volume 1, number 28, page 4:
quote.text: But somehow, despite wooden, unfunny dialogue, rigid characterization, and the dreadful mindless meaninglessness of it all, Good News manages to divert us for its three hours.

definitions.definition: (obsolete, intransitive) To turn aside; to digress.

quote.citation: 1641 September 7 (Gregorian calendar), John Evelyn, “[Diary entry for 28 August 1641]”, in William Bray, editor, Memoirs, Illustrative of the Life and Writings of John Evelyn, […], 2nd edition, volume I, London: Henry Colburn, […]; and sold by John and Arthur Arch, […], published 1819, →OCLC:
quote.text: I diverted to see one of the prince's palaces.
